stories.headline: Penn State Awards Its One Millionth Degree
stories.summary: Penn State handed out roughly 2,700 diplomas at its summer commencement on August 15, crossing the one-millionth-degree mark since the university's first graduates in 1861. It becomes only the third U.S. university, after Michigan and Indiana, to reach the milestone.
stories.narrative:
On a Saturday in mid-August, Penn State's University Park campus filled with families, gowns, and mortarboards for what turned out to be more than an ordinary commencement. Somewhere among the roughly 2,700 students crossing the stage that day, one graduate became the millionth person in the university's history to receive a Penn State degree, a threshold the school has been counting toward since its very first class of eleven students earned bachelor's degrees in agriculture back in 1861.

The university deliberately chose not to single out which graduate actually represents the millionth degree. Administrators said they didn't want to put that kind of spotlight on one student when the moment really belongs to everyone who has ever walked across a Penn State stage, from the school's origins as the Farmers' High School in 1855 through today's sprawling network of campuses across Pennsylvania.

Only two other American universities, Michigan and Indiana, have ever reached a million graduates, which gives some sense of how unusual the milestone is even among large, long-running public universities. Penn State president Neeli Bendapudi called it a moment that honors the legacy of everyone who came before while pointing to the university's ongoing commitment to its students, and Board of Trustees chair David Kleppinger framed it as proof of Penn Staters' broader commitment to the communities they go on to serve.

The milestone rippled well beyond campus. Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro issued a statewide proclamation marking the occasion, and local officials in State College and Centre County followed with their own recognitions. The Berkey Creamery, Penn State's beloved on-campus ice cream operation, even rolled out a limited-edition flavor chosen by the university community to celebrate, with the winning flavor set to stick around through the fall semester.

It's the kind of number that's easy to read past in a headline but hard to really picture: a million individual people, across more than sixteen decades, walking out of Penn State with a degree in hand and going on to become teachers, engineers, farmers, doctors, and everything in between. For a public university built to serve a whole state, crossing that threshold is a quiet but real measure of just how much ground it has covered.

stories.headline: New Radiation-Free Lung Scan Could Help Doctors Spot Disease in Children Sooner
stories.summary: Researchers at the University of Sheffield have developed an MRI technique using inhaled hyperpolarized xenon gas to image children's lungs in detail without any radiation exposure. Sheffield Children's Hospital is now using it to catch functional lung disease in cystic fibrosis patients earlier than ever before.
stories.narrative:
For children with chronic lung conditions like cystic fibrosis, keeping track of how their lungs are doing has traditionally meant repeated CT scans, each one delivering a dose of radiation to a young, still-developing body. Doctors have long known this was a real trade-off: the scans catch problems, but the cumulative radiation exposure over years of monitoring is its own quiet risk. A team at the University of Sheffield's POLARIS research group has now found a way around that problem entirely.

Their method uses a specially prepared form of xenon gas, hyperpolarized so that it shows up vividly on an MRI scanner. A child simply breathes it in, holds their breath for a few seconds while the machine captures images, and breathes it back out. There's no ionizing radiation involved at any point. Professor Jim Wild, who leads the research group, described the process in almost casual terms, but what it produces is anything but simple: detailed pictures of how air is moving through the lungs, how blood flow and gas exchange are functioning, and where structural problems might be hiding, all from a scan that takes only minutes and, with newer refinements, sometimes just seconds.

That speed matters enormously for pediatric patients, who often struggle to stay still through longer imaging sessions. It also means the scan can pick up on functional problems, changes in how well the lungs are actually working, that routine tests can miss even when a CT scan might look unremarkable. For a disease like cystic fibrosis, where early intervention can meaningfully change a child's long-term trajectory, catching that kind of subtle deterioration sooner is a real clinical advantage, not just a safer version of the status quo.

Sheffield Children's Hospital has already begun using the technique, marking a UK first for this kind of early functional lung disease detection in cystic fibrosis patients. It's a shift that lets clinicians monitor these children as often as their condition requires without the mounting radiation tally that used to come with that vigilance, and it offers a template that could extend to other chronic pediatric lung conditions well beyond cystic fibrosis.

It's easy to overlook how much of medical progress comes not from a single dramatic cure but from making existing good care safer and more sustainable to deliver. A scan that once carried a hidden cost now carries none, and that changes the calculus for every family whose child will need years of careful watching.

stories.headline: 97-Year-Old Doctor Is Overwhelmed to Attend Great-Granddaughter's Med School Graduation, 60 Years After His Own
stories.summary: Dr. Westel Creager promised his great-granddaughter Haiden Hauret that if she went to medical school, he would attend her graduation and help her into her first white coat. She enrolled at the University of Kentucky, the same school he graduated from six decades earlier, and this summer he kept his promise.
stories.narrative:
Some promises take decades to come due. Years ago, 97-year-old Dr. Westel Creager told his great-granddaughter Haiden Hauret that if she ever followed him into medicine, he would be there for her graduation, and he would personally help her put on her first white coat, just as someone had done for him. Haiden took him up on it. She enrolled at the University of Kentucky's medical school, the very same institution where her great-grandfather earned his own degree sixty years earlier, and this summer she graduated.

Her family made sure Westel had a crisp white doctor's coat to wear to the ceremony, a quiet echo of the one he wore decades ago walking out of the same halls. When he put it on, he became visibly emotional. "I'm overwhelmed," he said, and then he watched as his great-granddaughter received her own white coat, becoming the first of his descendants to follow him into the profession he spent a lifetime in.

Westel's own path into medicine wasn't an easy or obvious one. He grew up in poverty and returned to school as an older student to become a doctor, a decision that shaped the rest of his working life. He went on to spend decades practicing emergency medicine, still working in ERs into his seventies, tending to underserved communities long after most people would have called it a career. His granddaughter Kristi Johnson, Haiden's aunt, helped bring the extended family together to witness the moment their two generations of doctors finally overlapped.

What makes the story land isn't just the neat symmetry of two graduations sixty years apart at the same school. It's the fact that a 97-year-old man who spent his life treating other people's emergencies got to sit in an audience and watch his own family carry that work forward, and got to be the one to hand off the coat. His advice to anyone listening was simple and lived-in: you are never too old, keep taking the stairs, keep adding new hobbies, and keep changing your path if you need to.

Haiden now begins her own medical career carrying her great-grandfather's legacy with her, quite literally the second person in her family to wear that coat out of that particular building. It's a small story in the scheme of things, but it's the kind of family promise kept that reminds you how far one person's choices can ripple, sixty years and one more generation down the line.

stories.headline: China's Air and Water Quality Keep Improving Through Mid-2026
stories.summary: China's Ministry of Ecology and Environment reported that PM2.5 air pollution fell 6.2% and the share of good-quality surface water rose to 86.5% over the first seven months of 2026, compared with the same period last year. Officials credited sustained pollution-control and water-protection efforts.
stories.narrative:
Halfway into the year, China's environment ministry had some genuinely good numbers to share. Speaking at a press briefing, ecology and environment minister Huang Runqiu reported that average PM2.5 levels, the fine particulate pollution most closely linked to respiratory and cardiovascular harm, had fallen by 6.2 percent across the first seven months of 2026 compared with the same stretch of 2025. The share of days nationwide meeting official good-air-quality standards climbed by 3.9 percentage points over the same period.

The water figures told a similar story. Among the surface water sites the ministry monitors nationwide, rivers, lakes, and reservoirs used to track the country's overall water health, 86.5 percent were rated Class I to III, the country's designations for good-to-excellent quality, up 2.4 percentage points from a year earlier. That's a meaningful shift for a country that has spent years wrestling with industrial runoff and agricultural pollution in its waterways.

Officials attributed the gains to sustained enforcement of pollution controls and continued investment in water protection, rather than to any single new policy or one-off event. That steadiness is part of what makes the trend notable: this isn't a single clean month driven by favorable weather, but a continuation of improvement that's been building over recent years as China has pushed to clean up the air in its major cities and restore its rivers and lakes.

It's worth being clear-eyed about what these numbers do and don't capture. A national average can still mask serious pollution in particular cities or industrial regions, and self-reported government statistics deserve the same scrutiny any country's official data would get. But the direction of travel, cleaner air on more days, and more of the country's waterways meeting good-quality standards than the year before, is a real and measurable improvement for the roughly 1.4 billion people who breathe that air and rely on those rivers and lakes, in a country that has struggled with severe pollution for decades.

Environmental progress rarely arrives as a single dramatic breakthrough. More often it looks exactly like this: a percentage point here, a few micrograms less pollution there, reported quietly at a ministry briefing, adding up over years into cities where the sky is visibly clearer than it used to be.

stories.headline: Four More Rescued Beluga Whales Arrive at Chicago's Shedd Aquarium
stories.summary: Caspian, Peekachu, Rain, and Secord arrived at Shedd Aquarium on August 13 after being relocated from Marineland, the Canadian theme park that shut down in 2024. They bring the total number of rescued belugas at Shedd to eight, part of an international effort to rehome 30 whales after Canada banned keeping cetaceans in captivity for entertainment.
stories.narrative:
Eight years after Canada passed a law banning the breeding and entertainment use of captive whales, dolphins, and porpoises, the fallout from that decision is still playing out one relocation at a time. On August 13, four beluga whales named Caspian, Peekachu, Rain, and Secord arrived at Chicago's Shedd Aquarium, the second group to make the move from Marineland, the Ontario theme park near Niagara Falls that closed in 2024 and left dozens of whales in need of new homes.

The four new arrivals, ranging in age from 20 to 27, join four other belugas Shedd took in earlier this summer: Acadia, Osiris, Sierra, and Lillooet. That brings the aquarium's total to eight rescued whales, all of them female, all with existing bonds from their years together at Marineland. They're part of a far larger, unprecedented international undertaking to relocate 30 belugas and four dolphins out of the shuttered park to facilities in Georgia, San Diego, San Antonio, Spain, and Chicago.

Getting eight large, socially complex animals settled into a new three-million-gallon home isn't something that happens overnight. Shedd's care team is watching the whales around the clock in the Abbott Oceanarium, tracking everything from eating patterns to breathing rates to how the newcomers are interacting with each other and with staff. Charlie Jacobsma, the aquarium's behavior director, described the approach as deliberately unhurried: "This is a big transition, so we are taking this process hour-by-hour and day-by-day, at the whales' pace." Officials say the early signs have been encouraging, while cautioning that progress with animals adjusting to this kind of change doesn't always move in a straight line.

The rescue isn't finished. Shedd has said it remains committed to taking in up to two more belugas as the broader Marineland relocation effort continues, meaning this story of eight whales settling into their new home is really one chapter in a larger, ongoing effort to find every animal from that shuttered park somewhere safe to live out the rest of their lives.

It's a rescue built less on a single dramatic moment than on the accumulation of careful, unglamorous work: legislation passed years earlier, a coordinated relocation spanning two countries and multiple institutions, and now a team of caretakers learning the particular rhythms and personalities of eight whales one day at a time.

stories.headline: Teen Swimmer Completes Sixth of Seven Toughest Open-Water Swims in the World
stories.summary: 19-year-old Maya Merhige of Berkeley, California swam the Strait of Gibraltar on August 11 in just under four hours, her sixth completed leg of the Oceans Seven challenge. Only about 50 people worldwide have ever finished all seven swims, and Merhige is now one crossing away from becoming the youngest to do it.
stories.narrative:
There's a short list of open-water swims considered the hardest in the world, cold, current-choked crossings between continents and islands that together make up what's known as the Oceans Seven, swimming's answer to climbing's Seven Summits. Fewer than fifty people on the planet have ever completed all of them. On August 11, a 19-year-old from Berkeley, California moved to within a single swim of joining that short list.

Maya Merhige swam the Strait of Gibraltar, the narrow, heavily trafficked passage between Spain and Morocco where the Atlantic meets the Mediterranean, in 3 hours, 49 minutes, and 49 seconds. It was her sixth completed leg of the Oceans Seven, and she did it barely a month after finishing her fifth, the North Channel between Ireland and Scotland, in July. Her only remaining challenge is the Tsugaru Strait in Japan, which she's planning to attempt in 2027.

Merhige has been building toward this since she was fourteen. She swam the Catalina Channel in 2021, the Molokai Channel off Hawaii in 2023, the English Channel in 2024, New Zealand's Cook Strait in 2025, and the North Channel earlier this summer, each one notoriously difficult in its own way, from frigid water temperatures to unpredictable currents to, in the case of the Cook Strait, swarms of jellyfish she had to swim straight through. Along the way she's used her swims to raise awareness for cancer research through Swim Across America, turning grueling personal challenges into a platform for a cause.

What makes the Oceans Seven so punishing isn't just the distance of any single crossing but the range of conditions across all of them, water temperature, salinity, current, and sea state vary wildly from the Irish Sea to the Mediterranean to the strait separating Honshu and Hokkaido. Completing all seven demands a swimmer who can adapt to almost any water the world puts in front of them, which is part of why so few people ever finish the set.

If Merhige completes the Tsugaru Strait as planned, she'll become the youngest person ever to finish the Oceans Seven, still only in her early twenties with a feat behind her that most endurance athletes never attempt even once. For now, she has one crossing left, a stretch of cold Japanese water standing between her and a record that's taken most of her teenage years to build toward.

stories.headline: NASA Engineers a Power-Saving 'Big Bang' to Keep Voyager 2 Running Another Year
stories.summary: Facing dwindling power nearly 50 years after launch, NASA engineers simultaneously shut down and rewired several of Voyager 2's systems to free up roughly a year's worth of additional operating power. The same fix is now planned for Voyager 1, buying humanity's most distant spacecraft more time to keep sending data from interstellar space.
stories.narrative:
Voyager 2 has been flying for nearly fifty years, far longer than anyone who built it expected, and its plutonium power source has been quietly running down the entire time, losing about four watts of capacity every year as the fuel decays. By this year, mission engineers were staring down a familiar and unwelcome milestone: without some kind of intervention, they would have had to shut off yet another of the spacecraft's remaining science instruments before the end of 2026, one more silenced voice from the edge of the solar system.

Instead, NASA's team found a way to buy themselves time. In a maneuver they nicknamed the "Big Bang," engineers simultaneously powered down certain components on the spacecraft and swapped in lower-energy alternatives, all while keeping the craft's aging systems within the narrow thermal range they need to survive the cold of interstellar space. The result was roughly an extra year of operating power squeezed out of a spacecraft that already has almost nothing left to spare.

Voyager 2 now runs on just three of its original ten scientific instruments, after two were switched off back in 2024 on each of the twin Voyager probes to conserve power. Every watt matters at this point, which is what made project manager Suzanne Dodd's description of the trade-offs so pointed: "Every watt saved now is a decision about what data humanity still gets to learn from out there." It's a stark way of putting it, but an accurate one. Every instrument still running on Voyager 2 is actively returning data from a region of space no other spacecraft has ever reached, so keeping one more sensor alive for one more year is keeping open a window onto interstellar space that, once closed, closes for good.

NASA now plans to apply the same power-saving modifications to Voyager 1 in the coming months, extending the trick to both of the aging twins launched back in 1977. Neither spacecraft can be repaired or serviced, obviously, so every gain in operating life comes purely from clever engineering done from a distance of more than fifteen billion miles.

It's a modest-sounding fix, a bit of rewiring and a new nickname, but the stakes are anything but small. Voyager 2 remains the only object humanity has ever built to keep functioning and communicating from beyond the influence of our sun, and this quiet bit of ingenuity means it will keep doing that for at least another year.

stories.headline: Restored California Creek Helps Threatened Salmon Grow Twice as Fast and Doubles Their Survival
stories.summary: A restoration project turned a former lumber mill site on Prairie Creek, California, into wetlands and side channels where young coho salmon can rest and feed before reaching the ocean. Fish there grew up to twice as fast as those in the unrestored creek, and 2.6% of the 2023 cohort returned as adults to spawn, more than double the roughly 1% survival rate seen before.
stories.narrative:
Along California's redwood coast, a stretch of water called Prairie Creek has become one of the last refuges for three struggling salmon species: California Coastal Chinook, Northern California steelhead, and coho salmon, whose numbers have fallen by 90 percent over the past century. For decades the creek ran through the site of a former lumber mill, its natural floodplain cut off and its side channels filled in, leaving young fish with little food and few places to hide from predators or fast-moving water.

NOAA Fisheries and its partners set out to undo that damage, reconnecting the creek to its floodplain and rebuilding the wetlands, ponds, and slow-moving side channels that juvenile salmon depend on in their first months of life. The idea is simple: give young fish calmer water and more food, and they will grow bigger and stronger before they ever have to face the ocean.

The early results have exceeded what biologists expected. Carter Adamson, a fish biologist with the Pacific States Marine Fisheries Commission, found that in some sites and some years, juvenile coho using the restored habitat grew up to twice as fast as fish in the main creek. That extra size matters enormously, because bigger, stronger smolts are far more likely to survive the perilous transition to saltwater and the years they spend at sea.

The numbers bear that out. Among the coho salmon that hatched in 2023, 2.6 percent survived their time in the Pacific and returned to Prairie Creek as adults to spawn, more than double the roughly 1 percent survival rate researchers had documented before the restoration. For a species that has lost the vast majority of its historic population, that kind of gain is a meaningful step back from the brink.

Researchers with Cal Poly Humboldt and NOAA Fisheries plan to keep monitoring the creek through 2028 to see whether the gains hold up over time. But the early data offers a hopeful blueprint for other watersheds trying to bring depleted salmon runs back: sometimes the most effective fix isn't a hatchery or a fishing restriction, but simply giving a river back the slow water and hiding places it always used to have.

stories.headline: Once-Distrustful Rescue Horse Learns to 'Play' Guitar and Harp, Earning a Spot on a Debut Album
stories.summary: Yupia, a rescued horse with a troubled past at a Moorpark, California rescue facility, spent nine months distrusting people until singer-songwriter Mikayla Khramov began playing guitar near his pasture. He started nosing the strings to change the chords, and his sounds will now feature on two songs of her upcoming debut album.
stories.narrative:
When Mikayla Khramov started volunteering at a horse rescue in Moorpark, California, she met a seven-year-old Kentucky-bred horse named Yupia who wanted nothing to do with people. He had come to the rescue with behavioral issues and a deep-seated distrust that nine months of gentle, patient volunteering had barely begun to soften.

Khramov, a Los Angeles singer-songwriter, didn't try to win him over with treats or formal training exercises. Instead, one day she simply brought her guitar out to the pasture and started playing. What happened next surprised her: Yupia wandered over on his own, and instead of shying away, he began moving his mouth and snout across the strings, changing the chords as he went.

It kept happening. Whatever instrument she brought out, Yupia would approach and start experimenting with it, first strumming clumsily with his nose and, over time, working out how to press the strings with his teeth. When Khramov introduced her harp, he responded the same way, treating it like just another instrument to explore rather than something to fear.

For Khramov, the connection ran both directions. She has said the horse helped her fall back in love with music at a point when it had started to feel like a job rather than a passion. Rather than sessions that felt like obligations, her time with Yupia became something closer to play, a reminder of why she wanted to make music in the first place.

That partnership is now headed for a wider audience. Khramov is folding the sounds Yupia makes into two songs on her upcoming debut album, which blends Portuguese musicians with folk and electronic influences and is due out in September. What began as one horse slowly learning to trust a person with a guitar has turned into an unlikely creative collaboration, credited on the record for the part he played in making it.

stories.headline: Stress Hormone Discovered to Help the Brain Repair Itself After Injury
stories.summary: Researchers found that after brain injury, cells called oligodendrocyte progenitor cells release the stress hormone CRH near the damaged area, which helps guide those cells to mature and rebuild myelin, the protective insulation around nerve fibers. The discovery reveals a natural repair pathway and could point toward new treatments for brain damage.

stories.headline: Rescued Orangutans Released Into the Wild Are Now Raising Babies of Their Own
stories.summary: Nearly 200 rescued and rehabilitated Sumatran orangutans released into Indonesia's Jantho Pine Forest Nature Reserve over the past 15 years have successfully adapted to the wild, and at least 10 babies have now been born there. The births mark the establishment of an entirely new wild population of the critically endangered species.

stories.headline: Chester Zoo Hatches Five Secretarybird Chicks in Conservation First
stories.summary: Chester Zoo successfully bred secretarybirds for the first time in its 95-year history, with five chicks hatching to parents John and Jolene. With fewer than 6,700 secretarybirds left in the wild, the hatching is a major boost for the European breeding program, which produced only three other chicks elsewhere this year.

stories.headline: Ospreys Are Recovering in Britain Thanks to 'Pioneering Pairs' That Nest Far From Home
stories.summary: Researchers found that osprey recovery in Britain is being accelerated by independent-minded pairs that nest far from established populations, colonizing new territory rather than crowding existing sites. Conservationists are now using translocation and artificial nests to deliberately replicate this natural strategy and speed up the species' comeback.

stories.headline: 236-Million-Year-Old Fossil Suggests Mammal Ancestors Gave Birth to Live Young Far Earlier Than Thought
stories.summary: Paleontologists studying a cynodont fossil found a neonatal growth line and a newborn body size that match live-birth patterns seen in modern mammals rather than egg-layers, pushing back the known origin of live birth by roughly 95 million years. The find reshapes the story of how mammalian reproduction evolved.

stories.headline: Virginia Tech Security Guard Has Become a Local Celebrity for His Handmade Mini Rhino Trophies
stories.summary: Bryan Newton, a security guard at Virginia Tech's performing arts center, 3D-prints a custom themed mini rhino statue for every event as a prize in a staff guessing game, from a warrior rhino for a wrestling match to one in a witch hat for Halloween. The tradition has become a beloved keepsake that patrons and coworkers now look forward to collecting.

stories.headline: Fishing Guide's 911 Call Leads to Rescue of Entangled Manatee as Her Calf Watches
stories.summary: A fishing guide near St. Simons Island, Georgia, spotted an adult female manatee wrapped tightly in crab-trap line and called for help, triggering a two-day, multi-state response by Georgia DNR, Florida wildlife officials and the US Fish and Wildlife Service. The team freed her completely, fitted her with a satellite tag, and left her free to keep raising the dependent calf that stayed by her side throughout.

stories.headline: Scientists Discover Adult Brains Can Rebuild Their Own Damaged Support Cells
stories.summary: University of Zurich researchers found that astrocytes, brain support cells long thought unable to regenerate in adults, can send newly formed nuclei gliding across their extensions to repopulate tissue after injury. The discovery overturns a long-held assumption and points to new therapeutic targets for repairing brain damage and treating autoimmune neurological diseases.

stories.headline: Great Barrier Reef Gets a Reprieve as Monsoon Rains Cool the Water
stories.summary: A late monsoon season increased cloud cover and lowered sea temperatures this year, sparing the Great Barrier Reef the mass bleaching it suffered in 2024 and 2025. The Australian Institute of Marine Science's annual survey found coral cover actually rose 16.7% in the Northern Region and 10.2% in the Central Region, with 106 of 121 surveyed reefs showing moderate to high coral coverage.

stories.headline: Women's Professional Baseball Returns to the Field for the First Time Since 1954
stories.summary: The new Women's Professional Baseball League played its inaugural game in Springfield, Illinois, with 99-year-old Maybelle Blair — a veteran of the original All-American Girls Professional Baseball League — throwing out the first pitch despite recently broken ribs. The LA Queens beat the NY Heights to open a 30-game season, marking the first pro women's baseball competition in the US since the league that inspired 'A League of Their Own' folded in 1954.

stories.headline: Brown Student Spends Summer Helping Providence Teens Find Their Voice in English
stories.summary: Rising sophomore Justin Dunn spent four weeks teaching an English class for teens at the Providence Public Library through Brown University's SPRINT-iProv fellowship, taking students to a local market and having them build resumes so language skills stuck outside the classroom. Some of the library staff he worked alongside are immigrants who once learned English through the same program before returning to teach it themselves.

stories.headline: Rare 'Death Bloom' Agave Forces Botanical Garden to Cut Open Its Greenhouse Roof
stories.summary: A decade-old Agave sisalana at Birmingham Botanical Gardens in England has entered its once-in-a-lifetime 'death bloom,' with its flower spike growing so tall — over 18 feet — that horticulturists had to remove glasshouse ceiling panels to let it keep growing. The monocarpic plant is now producing hundreds of bulbils and seeds, plus four cloned 'pups,' to ensure new agaves carry on its genetic line after it dies.

stories.headline: Star Cluster Discovery Could Change How Scientists Measure the Universe
stories.summary: University of Missouri researchers found that the ratio of large to small stars varies depending on the environment where they form, challenging the long-held assumption that stars form in uniform proportions everywhere. The finding could improve how astronomers estimate galaxy mass and age, and may explain why some galaxies observed by the James Webb Space Telescope have looked more massive than expected.

stories.headline: Dogs' Brains Can Tell the Difference Between Fear and Sadness, Study Finds
stories.summary: Using brain scans, researchers from the University of Vienna, UNAM and Eotvos Lorand University found that dogs' brains respond differently to human faces showing fear versus sadness, the first evidence that dogs distinguish between specific negative emotions rather than just reading 'good' or 'bad.' Happy human faces lit up reward-related regions in the dogs' brains, hinting at just how finely tuned dogs are to their owners' feelings.

stories.headline: India Crosses 300 Gigawatts of Clean Power Capacity, Reaching 60% of Its 2030 Target
stories.summary: India's non-fossil fuel electricity capacity passed 300 GW as of July 31, 2026, now more than 54% of the country's total generation capacity. Solar power alone has grown from 2.8 GW in 2014 to nearly 165 GW today, putting the country past 60% of its goal to reach 500 GW of clean capacity by 2030.

stories.headline: Toddlers With Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy Show Rapid Motor Gains in New Drug Trial
stories.summary: In a Phase II trial, Binghamton University researchers gave the steroid-alternative drug vamorolone to boys aged 2 to under 4 with Duchenne muscular dystrophy. After just 12 weeks, gross-motor scores rose sharply with no serious side effects, raising hope that treatment can start before symptoms fully set in now that DMD has been added to newborn screening recommendations.

stories.headline: Team USA Smashes World U20 Record in Men's 4x100m Relay
stories.summary: At the World Athletics U20 Championships in Eugene, Oregon, the American quartet of Blake Hamilton, Dillon Mitchell, Kyler Brown and Tate Taylor ran 38.16 seconds to break the U20 world record in the men's 4x100m relay, beating the previous mark by more than a third of a second. Anchor Tate Taylor capped the meet with three gold medals.

stories.headline: Blind Dressage Horse Wins Competitions Using 'Equine Braille'
stories.summary: Milo, a 15-year-old Appaloosa who lost his sight to an eye condition, continues to compete successfully in dressage with rider Megan Share. The pair developed a tactile system of pressure cues so Milo can navigate the arena purely by feel, and he's now won the Royal Windsor Horse Show for the eighth year running.
